questions.q: What does TransformerLens's `HookedTransformer` provide that hand-written forward hooks from earlier lessons required manual work to get?
options: Named, indexed access to every internal activation, with `run_with_cache` returning every component's activations in one call instead of hand-rolled hooks per component
A way to train models without any activations at all
Automatic deletion of all attention heads
A completely different model architecture incompatible with GPT-style transformers
questions.explain: TransformerLens replaces one-off `register_forward_hook` boilerplate with a standard, named interface for every component's activations.

questions.q: What does sae_lens add specifically, compared to TransformerLens?
options: It replaces TransformerLens entirely for all hooking tasks
A tool exclusively for visualizing attention patterns, unrelated to SAEs
Shared infrastructure specifically for sparse autoencoders -- training new SAEs, loading pretrained ones, and generating feature dashboards
A dataset of labeled attention heads
questions.explain: sae_lens targets the Lesson 32 workflow specifically: training, sharing, and inspecting sparse autoencoders, rather than general activation hooking.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue shared tooling matters beyond just saving typing time?
options: It doesn't -- shared tooling is presented as purely a convenience with no other benefit
Because shared tooling eliminates the need for any research papers
Because results built on the same tested implementation are easier to reproduce, check against each other, and build on directly instead of re-deriving from scratch
Because it guarantees every experiment will produce identical results regardless of model
questions.explain: Common, tested libraries improve reproducibility and let the field build cumulatively rather than each project re-implementing the same hooking and patching logic.

questions.q: In the lesson's TransformerLens snippet, what does `cache["result", 5][:, :, 2, :]` retrieve?
options: The model's final output logits for the entire vocabulary
The loss value for layer 5
Layer 5, head 2's own isolated output -- the same kind of single-head contribution Lesson 30 captured by hand with a forward hook
A randomly initialized tensor unrelated to the model
questions.explain: This indexes into the cache for one specific head's output at one specific layer, exactly what the earlier hand-written hook code extracted manually.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how did interpretability research tooling change over time?
options: Tooling was shared libraries from the very first circuits papers, with no evolution
It moved from custom, one-off analysis code written for each specific paper toward shared, tested libraries like TransformerLens and sae_lens implementing the same core operations once
It has remained exactly the same bespoke, per-project scripts since the field began
All interpretability tooling has since been abandoned in favor of manual inspection only
questions.explain: Early papers relied on custom scripts; as core operations (hooking, caching, ablating, patching) recurred across projects, the field converged on shared libraries implementing them consistently.
